# Ratio·9

> A free, open-source guitar speed trainer and metronome built around
> subdivision ratio training. Two loops alternate between different
> subdivisions at one fixed BPM, so the ratio between them forces the speed
> jump instead of the tempo dial. Runs entirely in the browser, installs as a
> PWA, works offline, no account and no backend.

Site: https://ratio9.frankbirzle.de/
Source: https://github.com/frankbirzle/ratio9 (MIT)
Author: Frank Birzle. Non-commercial side project.

The trainer itself is a client-rendered single-page app, so this file carries
what its interface would otherwise hide. The articles are pre-rendered at build
time and can be fetched directly at the URLs listed below.

## What subdivision ratio training is

Set the click to 70 BPM. Play two bars of eighth-note triplets, three notes
per beat, then two bars of sextuplets, six notes per beat, without touching the
click. The pulse never moved and the picking hand just doubled its speed.

Getting from 210 to 420 notes per minute by tempo instead would mean dragging
the metronome from 70 to 140 BPM and surviving every broken tempo in between.
Changing the subdivision reaches the fast motion immediately, against a beat
that stays put, so when the fast pass drifts it is audible against a reference
that did not shift. The slow pass resets the motion, the fast pass pushes it.

## Modes

- **Ratios** — two loops, two subdivisions, one fixed BPM. Loop 2's length is
  derived from loop 1 so both loops carry the same number of notes (2 beats of
  8th triplets against 1 beat of sextuplets); the link can be switched off for
  independent beat counts. Configurable rest beats between the loops so the
  picking hand can reset, a count-in before the first round, an optional
  build-up that grows the phrase 2:1, 4:2, 6:3, 8:4 one set of rounds at a
  time, and an optional tempo ramp that steps the BPM up after every set.
- **Speed** — progressive tempo. The BPM ramps automatically after N bars along
  one of four curves: linear, logarithmic, stepback and pyramid.
- **Metronome** — a straight click: 8 subdivisions, 7 time signatures,
  configurable accent grouping.

## Sound

Nine engines, synthesized in the Web Audio graph at click time rather than
loaded as samples (only rim shot and tabla use samples, both CC0). The default,
Super Click, voices its three tiers separately instead of just louder and
higher: 1237 Hz accents, 996 Hz on-beats, 825 Hz subdivisions, each a short FM
beep with its own length and attack. Accents, beats and subdivisions have
independent volume, and subdivision clicks can be switched off.

## Practice tooling

Saved presets in localStorage, tap tempo, a countdown practice timer, an in-app
field manual, and keyboard shortcuts (Space start/stop, 1/2/3 modes, T tap
tempo, arrow keys tempo, S setup, Esc close). Amber-on-dark UI with
reduced-motion support.

## The method, in order

Add one variable at a time.

1. One note, one string, picking hand only. Ratios at a slow tempo, 2 beats each way.
2. Extend the fast pass: 2 beats, then 4, then 8.
3. Add the fretting hand. Synchronisation only, picking hand stays relaxed.
4. Three notes. Back to 2 beats, build to 8.
5. Extend up the scale, including position shifts.
6. Only then raise the tempo, and rebuild from one note, because the fast
   motion is a different motion.

## Articles (the field manual)

Index: https://ratio9.frankbirzle.de/articles

- [Why I built a ratio trainer instead of another metronome](https://ratio9.frankbirzle.de/articles/why-i-built-a-ratio-trainer):
  a book about talent hotbeds, five YouTube guitarists saying variations of the
  same thing, and a plateau that would not move.
- [The three zones, and why only one of them builds speed](https://ratio9.frankbirzle.de/articles/the-three-zones):
  comfort, edge of ability, speed burst. Most players spend a whole session in
  the wrong one.
- [The myelin story, and what actually survives scrutiny](https://ratio9.frankbirzle.de/articles/the-myelin-story):
  the "perfect reps wrap myelin around the circuit" claim, and why the evidence
  is thinner than the guitar internet suggests.
- [How I actually use the speed trainer](https://ratio9.frankbirzle.de/articles/how-i-use-the-speed-trainer):
  the exact routine, start to finish.
- [Linked loops, a slow ramp, and letting the app run my routine](https://ratio9.frankbirzle.de/articles/linked-loops-and-a-slow-ramp):
  loop 2 follows loop 1 so both loops carry the same number of notes, the
  phrase grows 2:1, 4:2, 6:3, 8:4 on its own, and the tempo steps up two beats
  per minute after every set of rounds.

## Technical

React 19 and TypeScript on Vite 8, React as the only runtime dependency. No
backend, no API keys, no analytics, no third-party requests (fonts are
self-hosted). The audio scheduler uses lookahead scheduling against
AudioContext.currentTime rather than timers, with a guard against catch-up
bursts when a background tab is throttled. Deployed as static assets on
Cloudflare Workers.

## Credits

The method is assembled from people who explain it better: NathanGuitar (the
direct inspiration for the ratios mode), Troy Grady on picking mechanics, and
JustinGuitar, Ben Eller, Bernth, Lukas Kocka and Matt Wright Music.
